3. Facts giving rise to this rule may briefly be stated thus: 

 11. Before the Court of Settlement the Respondent No. 2 did not file any written statement in controverting or denying the assertion made by the petitioner. But the Court of Settlement without considering the facts and circumstances of the case and without applying judicial mind passed an order dismissing the application by its judgment and order dated 5.4.87 vide annexure P to the petition. The finding of the Court of Settlement to the effect the perpetual lease created by Hari Ballav  Bashak in favour of Pir Mohammed vide perpetual lease deed dated 20.1.1960 in respect to the property in question is hit by the provision of section 75A of the SAT Act, 1950 is wholly misconceived and contrary to law inasmuch relevant gazette notification under the provision of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was published in the official Gazette on 1st August, 1963. Photostat copy of the same is annexed and marked as Annexure Q to the petition. The photostat copy of the Ministry letter dated 14.6.87 is annexed hereto and marked as Annexure 'R' to the petition. There being no other efficacious remedy provided in law against the impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement, petitioner invoked the writ jurisdiction and preferred this application. 

 12. Respondent No. 2, Secretary, Ministry of Works. Secretariat Building appeared and filed affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegation set out in the writ petition and stating therein that during war of liberation and after war the whereabouts of Syed Mosaheb Ali were not known and the property vested in the Govt. as abandoned under PO 16 of 1972. The sale deed alleged to have been executed and registered by Syed Mosaheb Ali in respect of the property in question is false, forged, without consideration and sham paper transaction and in the relevant period Syed Mosaheb All was not present in Bangladesh. Syed Mosaheb Ali's another property at 13, Bitarbari Lane was never abandoned and this property neither declared as abandoned property by relevant authorities of the Govt. and that he handed over peaceful possession of the aforesaid property to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and since then the petitioner has been possessing the said property as lawful owner are all denied. The properties of Syed Mosaheb Ali was rightly declared to be abandoned property and Syed Mosaheb Ali never handed over possession of the property to the petitioner on 12.2.74 and the petitioner has never been in possession of the property. So her eviction on 7.8.75 from the said property by officer of the respondent No. 2 is concoction. The petitioner made several representations before the Ministry of Works. The finding of the Court of Settlement to the effect that perpetual lease created by Hari Ballaw Bashak in favour of Pir Mohammad in respect of the property in question is hit by provision of section 75A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, that the statement made in paragraph 15 of the Writ Petition that the respondent No. 2 being emboldened by the aforesaid judgment of the Court of Settlement has decided to sell the property in question and to that effect issued a letter to the tenant and asking them to submit bids is denied. The property in question has been rightly declared as abandoned property. All other allegations set out in the writ petition have been categorically denied in the affidavit-in-opposition. 

 (i) 	any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 

 Explanation: "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 

 14. According to the definition 'abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh. It implies that there should be some information to the Govt. that the owner is outside Bangladesh but sub-clause II (a) further conveys the idea mere absence from Bangladesh will not render the property abandoned unless the activity of the owner of the property outside Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of the country. In other words the owner in the opinion of the Government by indulging in activity prejudicial to the interest of the State. Sub-clause 11 (a) of clause 1 of Article 2 is to be read with clause 1 of Article 2. In the case of M/s Speed Bird Navigation Vs. Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 170, their Lordships have expounded this provision of law holding that the clause referred above appears to be that the properties of those absentee owners about whose purpose of staying outside the country the Government has not yet formed any opinion whatsoever cannot be also regarded as abandoned properties, but the properties of those persons about whose purpose of staying abroad the Government has formed an adverse opinion, shall be deemed to be abandoned properties. This decision of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division which has been reported in 30 DLR (AD) page 101 and in that decision of their Lordships of the Appellate Division confirmed the view taken by their Lordships of the High Court Division and further held that the power regarding the formation of the opinion cannot be delegated to other Government officials. Their Lordships further held that" there cannot be any vesting of absentee owners of properties in the government unless there is Government's opinion expressed to the effect that his absence from the country is detrimental to the interest of the State."This definition clause is to be read as a whole in the light of the title and the preamble and also as an integral part of the Presidential Order. 

 16. Thus from this decision the conclusion that can be arrived at is that the owner must be absentee from the country and second, that the Government has expressed opinion that his absence from the country is due to a purpose prejudicial to the interest of the State. It is not possible to presume that the legislature had intended that any one absent from Bangladesh being not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh would be coming within the mischief of PO 16 of 1972 and the property thereof is to be taken as abandoned property. 

 17. Now it is to be seen if whereabouts of Syed Mosaheb Ali from whom petitioner purchased the property as per sale deed vide Annexure F dated 12.2.74 were not known. The expression where about of the owner not known implies that the properties are not in his possession and under his control and management and he is hiding in the country or has left Bangladesh. It should be mentioned here that many of the owners who collaborated with Pakistani Army left the country or want into hiding abandoning their property without making arrangement for administration of the said property. One living outside of the country will not render the property abandoned unless there is opinion from the Government that the activity of the owner outside the country is prejudicial to the State Syed Mosaheb Ali owned two premises one at 93 Bitar Bari Lane and another at holding No. 3 Bitar Bari Lane and both of his properties were never declared as abandoned or taken over as abandoned property by Government. The holding situated at 13 Bitar Bari Lane was not declared or taken over as abandoned properties though it was owned by Syed Mosaheb Ali. But the holding No. 3 was taken over as abandoned property despite the fact that Syed Mosaheb Ali never left the country and that he died on the soil of Bangladesh. In support of this contention -a death certificate of Syed Mosaheb Ali which is lying with the lower Court record was filed before the Court of Settlement. From the death certificate it appears that death of Syed Mosaheb Ali occurred on 13.3.76 and that place of death occurred at holding No. 3 Bitar Bari Lane. Since the petitioner was evicted from holding No. 3 Bitar Bari Lane on 7.8.75 by officers of Respondent No.2 and death of Syed Mosaheb Ali occurred on 13.3.76 ie after eviction, the learned Court of Settlement observed regarding the authenticity of the death certificate. It has already been referred above that Syed Mosaheb Ali owned two properties which were located side by side at 3 and 13 Bitar Bari Lane. From the death certificate of Syed Mosaheb Ali, it is evident that death of Syed Mosaheb Ali occurred in Bangladesh at holding No. 3. The learned Court of Settlement did not treat it to be the authentic document but no reason has been assigned to cast any aspersion regarding its genuineness. In absence of any attack regarding the authenticity of the death certificate it cannot be said that the entry made in the death certificate was not correct. It appears from the death certificate that death of Mosaheb Ali occurred on the soil of Bangladesh. 

 23. Evidence on record proves affirmatively that petitioner Syed Mosaheb Ali died in Bangladesh and there is no material on record to warrant inference that Syed Mosaheb Ali even if presumed to have left Bangladesh indulged in activity prejudicial to the interest of the State. Therefore, the property in question does not fall within the mischief of definition of abandoned property. This aspect of the matter was not considered by the learned Court of Settlement.
